utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you and good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-67-T, the Prosecutor versus Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. This is Tuesday, and I welcome the representatives of the OTP, Mr. Seselj, and everyone helping us. I would first like to ask Mr. Seselj whether his health is sufficiently good to follow this hearing.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: ... makes it possible for me to attend hearings. It has never happened so far that hearings could not be held because of my health.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you, Mr. Seselj. Before giving you the floor and giving the floor to the Prosecutor, who also needs about 20 minutes, I would like to say the following: First, the Trial Chamber is now seized of a number of motions, of pending motions. There are eight of them, and in the days to come, we will very quickly rule on these. For your information, let me remind you that the oldest motion dates back to April 9, 2009. It is an OTP motion for the admission, under Rule 92 quater, of a number of documents regarding Milan Babic, and the Trial Chamber will soon rule on this because deliberations have already occurred. Secondly, another Prosecution motion on VS-010, VS-011, VS-017, VS-026, and VS-032, and VS-034, and this pending motion will also be ruled upon, since the deliberations have already been made. Third motion, dated May 5th, 2010, it's a Prosecution motion for the admission of 15 intercepts. The Trial Chamber has also deliberated on this and will soon rule on this. We also have two pending motions on the admission of a number of documents, notably interviews or speeches made by the accused. This is the -- it's a Bar Table motion. The Judges have also deliberated on this, and a decision will be issued very soon. Then a motion dated June 1st on the admission of 16 documents. There, again, the Judges have deliberated, and a decision is pending. Then another motion on the admission, under 92 ter, of two statements made by the OTP, members of the OTP. Deliberations have also been made on this matter, and a decision will soon be rendered. Then another motion on documents concerning Witness VS-026. The Trial Chamber will soon be able to issue its decision. Furthermore, we also have one last OTP motion regarding a request for disclosure of exchange of mail between myself and the President of this Tribunal. The Trial Chamber has deliberated and has decided that this is not relevant in our case, which is to try Mr. Seselj for facts which occurred in the 1990s. We will soon render a decision on grounds of lack of relevance, and it will be a written decision, of course, with -- and the motivations will be given in this decision. So this settles it for the pending motions. Now, for Mr. Seselj's personal information regarding translation time and so on, the trial -- I would like to say that today the Trial Chamber has filed a redacted decision on the funding of Mr. Seselj's defence. Let me just read the disposition, without going into the grounds, because there is 27 paragraphs. This is what I say: The Trial Chamber, in application of Rule 54 of the Rules and Article 21(B) of the Statutes, orders, proprio motu, the Registrar, as of today, as of November 2nd, and until the end of the trial, to fund 50 per cent, 5-0, 50 per cent of the funds allocated, in principle, to a totally indigent accused, to the Defence team for the accused, consisting of three privileged associates, a case manager and an investigator, based on the scheme for persons assisting indigent self-represented accused and on the basis of a determination of the complexity of this case at Level 3, unless other information is provided. In this disposition, this is added: Judge Lattanzi attaches a separate opinion to this decision. And this has to do with whether this was proprio motu or not. So Judge Lattanzi will write her own decision, her own submissions on this, which is, of course, marginal compared to the essential element, which is that the Trial Chamber has decided that 50 per cent of Mr. Seselj's defence will be funded. The decision will soon be translated, and you will be able to read it. Furthermore, Mr. Seselj, lately I've been receiving personal mail. I don't know why. Let me remind you that there are three Judges on this Bench, so if I get mail, I would like my colleagues to be cc'd, at least, on it or to also be recipients of this mail. But I received a personal letter. Since this was a personal -- this was personal mail, I can either talk about it or not. I received a personal -- some personal mail from your associate, Mr. Mirovic, Dejan Mirovic, sending me a document, which was translated, which seems to be addressed to the UN Security Council, unless I'm wrong, and your associate, in this 17-page letter, is mentioning all points that have to do with your trial, the fact that your detention is arbitrary, that your rights are infringed upon, that this is not a public trial. He mentions also your hunger strike, the 15 months sentence you received for contempt of court, et cetera, et cetera. So this is my question, Mr. Seselj: I'd like to know whether you were aware that this person, that this associate, has seized the Security Council. I would like to know also whether it was the Security Council that was seized. And I would like to know what I'm supposed to do with this letter.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you expect me to respond to this question straight away, I would like to say that I wanted to say something about your decision about financing the Defence, because I received that decision today, an hour before I left the prison. Or do you want me to answer your question related to Dejan Mirovic's letter?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I would rather have you answer first, and then we'll come back to the decision on funding.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dejan Mirovic, my legal adviser, indeed did send a letter to the Security Council, and he personally delivered the text of that letter, translated into the English and Russian languages, to the ambassadors of the permanent members of the Security Council in Belgrade, and he also sent it in a certain way directly to the Security Council. The essence of this letter has to do with the abuse of law and legal proceedings with regard to witness protection, and primarily inventing a new crime, according to Rule 77; that is to say, disclosing the identity of protected witnesses. That does not exist in any single normal legal system anywhere in the world. It cannot be punishable by seven years in prison. And a person who already stands accused of the most serious war crimes cannot additionally be tried for having disclosed to the public the names of protected witnesses. Somebody has to control The Hague Tribunal institutionally as well. Truth to tell, this kind of control or check has not been envisaged by its own Rules of Procedure and Evidence, but no court can function without this kind of control. As lawyers, if we try to look at this, who it is that could exercise this kind of control over The Hague Tribunal, there is a self-evident answer: It is only the Security Council, which established it in the first place, to leave aside the fact that there is no one to exercise any kind of control over the Security Council and to stop it from establishing illegal courts. But this did happen, the Security Council did establish an illegal court, and now we have to see what should be done with this illegal court. They cannot, though, invent new crimes. The question of respect of law in court cannot be established as an inherent right of a court. However, if the Statute of The Hague Tribunal does not envisage how this is going to be resolved, there is an international legal code. The highest code, the upper-most code that exists in criminal law to date is the Statute of Rome and the Rules based on that Statute, and also a separate legal document that describes particular crimes. The Rome Rules of Procedure and Evidence does not stipulate at all that there is that kind of a violation or crime such as disclosing the name of a protected witness or identity of a protected witness. A witness has to testify in public, in court, under his or her full name and surname, and then if the witness is in any kind of jeopardy after having testified, then appropriate authorities should do their best to protect that person, to relocate him, to find for him and his family a new environment where they would live, and so on. That is the essence of Dejan Mirovic's letter, and of course he wrote that letter in agreement with myself. As a matter of fact, the original idea was my own, and I stand by that letter. Now, after the letter was sent to ambassadors and delivered in person to some of them in Belgrade, Mr. Mirovic decided to inform the President of The Hague Tribunal about this and the President of the Trial Chamber involved in this case. It is a letter that is open to the public. It is not marked as confidential in any way. So the letter was sent to you, Mr. President, on the assumption that you would familiarise your colleagues with the content of the letter. It is not a formal filing by the Defence, because a formal filing by the Defence can only be made by myself, personally. This letter is just a piece of information. I think it's better for you to have been informed of the fact that we sent this kind of letter to the Security Council rather than if we hadn't done that. We expected to inform your colleagues about this, and we expect the President of The Hague Tribunal to familiarise all the Judges of The Hague Tribunal with this letter. Why not? So this is a matter of principle. The letter only contains legal argument, legal argument exclusively. It is -- it has been made public in Serbia. It has been published in its entirety in the top newspaper, that is to say, the paper "Velika Srbija," "Great Serbia." There is no reason for you not to familiarise your colleagues with its content. What is described there are just some of the things, imposing a lawyer on the accused and many other things, and this is just an introduction by way of an illustration. The letter focuses on the invention of a specific crime by the Judges of this Tribunal, something that they certainly had no right to do. And once the Statute of Rome was passed as the top-ranking legal code, in international terms, to this day, The Hague Tribunal had to adapt all of its own founding documents to that and pretend to be legal and legitimate, at least a bit, in that way, since it hadn't been founded as a legal and legitimate court in the first place. Now, why The Hague Tribunal did not do that, that is something we are going to discuss in professional international circles, and that is why we sacrificed a certain amount of money and had the letter -- and had this letter translated into the English language. I hope that its quality suffices for our purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You explained everything about this letter, and now I would like to deal with one penultimate subject, which is your health. I also received a confidential letter from your close associate, Mr. Aleksic, but you always said that everything that has to deal with your health is not confidential. So I can say that your associate told me about your state of health. Now, as you know better than anyone, actually - I think I understood that yesterday you had some surgery - after the surgery your wife said that you were concerned about the post-surgery care which was not done at the jail -- not done at the hospital but at the jail, which was insufficient. And Mr. Mirovic also spoke in the Serbian press in order to give his point of view on this. Let me remind you that the Trial Chamber is fully aware of the problem, to the extent that, in a decision, we ordered for a panel of experts to examine you, and we want this panel of experts to tell us what exactly is your health situation and whether you're fit to stand trial. So we asked for this panel of international experts, and I insist on the word "international," experts, be carried out as expediently as possible. Now, the fact that you're in the courtroom today proves that you're doing well. You had the surgery a few days ago, and you're here with us. But I note that your wife seemed extremely worried, as well as your associates. Two associates actually intervened. Mr. Aleksic, through a letter, a letter which I will forward to the President of the Tribunal, because in this letter there is the -- there is mention of the fact that a number of Serbian detainees passed away in jail or right after being in jail, but -- so I will forward this letter to the President of the Tribunal, because I do not feel competent over this. My only competence, as well as the competence of my fellow Judges, is to make sure that you are as healthy as possible to defend yourself, and to self-represent yourself, and to fully exercise your rights. As of today, we are awaiting this letter of expertise, this expert medical evaluation. It's an international panel. They have to meet, they have to discuss all the documents, and then they also have to examine you, so that will probably take some time. But we will soon have this expert medical evaluation made by international experts. So that is what I had to say on your health. And now my last subject before giving you the floor: Scheduling. I'm sure you want to know exactly where we stand now. Now, regarding scheduling issues, as you know, today we're in a standby mode. On the one hand, we're waiting for the filing of the experts on the Mladic diaries. We would like to know whether the Mladic diaries were actually written by his own hand or whether anything was added later on. And an expert has been appointed, and he will answer all our questions, but we cannot do anything while we are still awaiting this expertise. We cannot go forward regarding Rule 98 bis. Furthermore, we have one -- we still have one pending witness, VS-026. I will not mention his name; he's protected. But up until now, he was not available, and an expert had noted and certified that he was not available, but now, just by miracle, obviously, he's healthy again. We checked this miracle, because we really asked an expert to look into this, and we're waiting for the feedback from this expert. So if the expert says that he is fit to testify, probably through a videolink which will be organised, of course, that's one thing; and if he's not fit to testify, then we will admit his statement under Rule 92 ter [as interpreted]. We'll admit his previous statements as well as the statements he gave to your Defence. Then once this is over, we will move to the Rule 98 bis procedure, and we have a scheduling order for the organisation of this hearing. This is how things stand now. Correction on page 10, line 11: It is not "92 ter," but "92 quater." Nothing escapes the Judges, even a small detail, because there's a big difference between "ter" and "quater." So I think we took stock of the situation, as far as the Bench is concerned, unless my colleagues would like to take the floor. It seems that this is not the case. So, Mr. Seselj, now you have the floor, and, of course, feel free to address this issue of financing.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for my -- the condition of my health, I initially pointed out that it has never jeopardised the trial so far, and that won't be the case in the future. As long as I can breathe, I will be able to actually participate in the trial, and you don't need any international experts to ascertain that. However, as you have mentioned, articles in the newspapers and the statements of my wife, Jadranka Seselj, as well as the letter that you received from my legal adviser, Boris Aleksic, I must communicate some things to you. More than ever, I am now convinced that somebody from the outside is manipulating the condition of my health. Two days ago, Nerma Jelacic, the speaker of the Tribunal, gave a statement for the media, probably at a press conference, that my operation on last Thursday was completed without any complications. That is nothing but a lie. Ms. Jelacic lied to the public. During that operation, which lasted three hours, at a certain moment I lost consciousness. That is a very serious complication for an operation of this kind, because this operation is carried out without full anaesthesia. It's a heart surgery, but the chest is not opened, but the heart is accessed through the blood vessels from the groins. The surgeon also informed me later on that I suffered from lack of oxygen and that they had to give me additional oxygen. That, too, is a serious complication. But the worst thing is that I never found out whether the operation was successful or not. Why did I have to be operated upon under a false name? Nobody informed me of it until I arrived there and until I found myself in bed. If I had been informed in prison that I would be operated upon under a false name, I wouldn't have gone there. But having already been there, I thought, okay, let's go through it, and later on I'll raise hell about why this had to be done under a false name. I am proud of my personal name, and I am proud of being indicted of war crimes by the ICTY. I am also proud that I'm being transported through The Hague with shackles on my hands. I'm proud of my shackles, and I won't allow anybody to manipulate me this wait. Everything I do and everything that happens to me must happen under my full name. And a day after the operation, long ultrasound examinations were carried out, ultrasounds of the heart and the chest. When I asked about the results, they said, The professor will let you know. But when will the professor come? At 10.00. But the professor never arrived. I left the hospital. The report about that operation has still not been forwarded to the Detention Unit clinic, and nothing is known yet. Maybe it was successful, but then my question is: Why do I still feel the same symptoms? When I arrived at the Detention Unit, I immediately went to the clinic, where I was received by the chief doctor, Dr. Paulus Falke, with two nurses, and I mentioned all these suspicious circumstances to them. I said what was happening, and I said probably the operation was unsuccessful because they didn't say anything to me, they avoided the answer. But the surgeon who operated on me said that they couldn't know if they had been successful and that it would be known only in three or four months. That was suspicious to me as well. Dr. Falke said to me to lie down on the bed to have an ECG performed. The nurse did the ECG, and she was appalled by the result. She said, Some electrode must have fallen off. She checked all the electrodes, but they were all there. She did it again, and the results were again incredibly bad. Then Dr. Falke said, The ECG device is broken, but in these eight years, this has never happened before. And I wanted to see the result. You know that long -- long band of paper. And what I always want to see is a diagnosis which is printed out by the computer at the end. And I see five things are irregular. I don't speak Dutch, so I can't know what it's about, but I did hear that the doctor and the nurse were whispering to each other in Dutch, and I recognised the word "extrasystole." I know what "asystole" is and a "diastole" from my high school days, so I know what an "extrasystole" is. So there must be a disturbing factor causing arrhythmia. And I tell them, The device is not broken, and they said to me, Yes, it is. So Friday, Saturday, Sunday go by, and Monday comes. I always have the same symptoms, and today I'm taken to the same ECG, the very same one. And I was fooling around with the nurses all the time and with the assistant doctor, How is it fixed without ever having seen a repairman? And the ECG now shows bradycardia, that my pulse was around 40. A short while ago, when I was brought to the Tribunal, I immediately wanted to see the Tribunal's doctor, to have him take my pulse. And he said, Now it's 54, which is almost normal, but there's arrhythmia again. And this concealing of the real medical finds is not something that is done to me, exclusively. It was done to General Vladimir Lazarevic all the time. It happened constantly to Jovica Stanisic, and happened constantly with Nebojsa Pavkovic, and some others. These three are in the same block as I, so I have been an eye-witness to the fact that this has been happening to them constantly. The doctors are treating us as if we were even bigger idiots than they are, which I assure you is not true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, the Bench discovered that you had surgery under a false name, but this was perhaps for security reasons. We don't know why they decided to send you there under a false name. Perhaps they wanted to protect you from the media or from somebody else. Secondly, we are not medical experts. This is why we asked for a medical expert. What is important is that you are alive, and you are living proof of that because you are here today. According to what you say, you still suffer from arrhythmia, which would explain why the nurse and the doctor were surprised by the results. But as you said yourself, and the surgeons said, that we would see things more clearly in three or four months, so I think the best thing to do is to wait until we get the results from this medical evaluation. But, of course, you can also ask for the operation report to be sent to you, because when surgery is done, a report is produced, and in this report there should be a reason mentioned for why you lost consciousness. There must be a reason for that. And if it was due to a lack of oxygen, one should hope that your brain was fully supplied by blood. Otherwise, there could be an issue. So perhaps you can deal with the doctor and explain to him what you said to us. We are not medical experts. I gave you the floor in order to have a full picture of the situation, and it seems that you are still encountering some problems. Given that everything that you said is in a transcript, and the Registry is following, minute after minute, what you're saying, I'm sure that while I'm speaking some phone calls are being made between the Registry and the doctor in order to check all this. Perhaps we can move to another topic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I have to clarify this question pertaining to the letter that you got from my legal adviser, Boris Aleksic. Boris Aleksic sent you a letter in order to inform you about the behaviour of Ken Roberts, Deputy Registrar. Ken Roberts, on the 20th of October, addressed Boris Aleksic because in the "Politika" newspaper, Aleksic, as Ken Roberts said, insinuated that my medical treatment in The Hague does not meet even basic prerequisites and that my health was seriously in danger, and also he referred to the opinion of Russian medical specialists, who believe that the doctor in The Hague Tribunal prison had an effect on the death of Slobodan Milosevic and also that there had been manipulations with the late Mr. Milosevic. And now this Ken Roberts, who thinks he is somebody, some kind of a relevant factor, said that these are groundless statements and could diminish the trust of the international public towards the International Tribunal and its staff. This International Tribunal never enjoyed any kind of reputation, so that is totally wrong. As soon as it was established, there were objections voiced about the way in which it had been established, and nothing more than that, especially because such horrible things happened here that should never be repeated again, if an international criminal judiciary survives at all after the experiences of the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia. And now this Deputy Registrar is worried because Boris Aleksic perhaps violated the Code of Conduct for Defence Counsel, and he signed the obligation to respect these provisions. And then Ken Roberts says, Please bear in mind that on account of such violations, privileged status could be taken away from you, the one that you enjoy as legal adviser to Mr. Seselj, or proceedings -- disciplinary proceedings could be initiated against you. First of all, how can disciplinary proceedings be instituted against a legal adviser? Who can do that? Only I can do that. He is my legal adviser, and nobody else can do that. Whatever Ken Roberts does, or his boss, John Hawking, Boris Aleksic remains my legal adviser. No one from the outside can dismiss my legal advisers. However, like until now, they can hinder my communication with my legal advisers and members of my team. That, they can do. That is what this Tribunal has been doing for all of eight years. First, for seven months, and after that, for another two months, I could not even telephone my family, let alone receive visitors or contact members of the team assisting my defence. In this context, Mr. President, Boris Aleksic wrote to you. He informed you about that. He informed you about what was going on in the case of the death of Mr. Milosevic, who was killed here. He was certainly killed here. He was killed at least by denying him appropriate care by a physician, because a few days before his death, in this very same courtroom he said that he felt as if his head had weighed half a ton, he asked for medical treatment, and the Presiding Judge brutally interrupted him then and even said that he was sick and tired of him. That's what he said, I've had enough of you, I'm sick and tired of you. That is what happened in this courtroom, before the eyes of the public. How can that be concealed? Milan Kovacevic was tormented throughout the night and died before daybreak. Everybody knew what kind of problems he had with his heart. Slavko Dokmanovic was ill for months before he committed suicide. He had a psychological condition. Everybody knew that he had a psychiatric condition, everybody knew that he had a diagnosis, and psychiatrists came and treated him. Somebody has to be held responsible for his death as well. If interventions could be made -- if interventions had been made by treating his depression, he would not have been -- he would not have committed suicide. Later on, we realised through these proceedings as well that had Slavko Dokmanovic had nothing to do whatsoever with any crimes in Ovcara, and that one witness who testified in public here in this courtroom, and who was a victim, too, actually thought that he had recognised Slavko Dokmanovic in a uniform of a lieutenant-colonel of the air force, and in actual fact this was a security officer who was wearing an air force uniform, and he came from the 1st Military District. He was in Ovcara, but he was never held accountable for that crime. And now it seemed to the witness that that had been Slavko Dokmanovic. So those were the grounds for indicting Slavko Dokmanovic, there you go, and that is the reason why he committed suicide. Then there was the case of Djordje Djukic, who was held here without any proper grounds until it became perfectly clear that he would die. Then he was released, he went to Belgrade, and he died a month later. As for General Momir Talic, the very same thing happened. Well, look, when Milan Babic hanged himself, I was the first one to present in my motion the fact that he left a farewell letter. The Tribunal officially stated that there was no farewell letter, and then it turned out, after all, that there was a farewell letter. What was established was that the width of the bruise around his neck did not correspond to the width of the belt that he allegedly used to hang himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecutor wants to take the floor, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution respectfully submit that this is not an appropriate use of the time of the Tribunal and an administrative hearing. This has nothing to do with any administrative issues. The accused has now, for the last five or ten minutes, gone on and on about conspiracy theories against the Tribunal. If he has any administrative points to make from this, he should make it now, and otherwise should move on to a proper point for this hearing. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, what do you have to say to the Prosecutor, who states that you are talking about conspiracy theory here?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not putting forward any sort of theory here. I am merely stating information that there are various conspiracies here and that they are not happening in my trial only, but that they have been known to happen earlier in other trials, and they are happening in some other trials that are going on parallelly. At the last status conference, I have publicly stated my position on this, because you cannot convict me, because you have no proof for any crime. Of course, you have to kill me, then. How do you get out of this case otherwise? There's no other way. I'm more than ever convinced that my medical condition is being manipulated from outside. I must die, but the medical documentation has to be clean because there must be no evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Please move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, I have to say, from a personal point of view, but I believe that my colleagues will share my point of view: If there was a conspiracy theory in which Judges were involved, because if I read between the lines, that's what you may imply, I was wondering whether I would have mentioned the letter from Mr. Aleksic, I was wondering whether I would have appointed independent medical experts to find out what is really going on, and I was wondering whether I would have allowed publicly for you to say this, if I was part of this conspiracy theory. If I was, I would have stopped you from talking, and we would have moved on. So I do hope that it is very clear in your mind that the Judges are not targeted by what you're saying about the conspiracy theory, because if that's what you're thinking, then I will stop the trial immediately, because I'm sure that you cannot think for one second that -- I could not take part in a trial where you would be a victim of any conspiracy within which I would be part.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I never said that. I haven't mentioned you or your colleagues, Mr. Harhoff and Ms. Lattanzi, by name as partakers to any conspiracy, but I'm stating to you what is happening at the ICTY and at the Detention Unit. I'm speaking the language of facts. I'm not pointing fingers to this or that person as being personally responsible for this or that, because I have no evidence for that. But my evidence are these material facts that cannot be denied. I have facts, and the general public can draw their conclusions from that, and so can you. Is that suspicious to you or not, that's another thing. To me, it's all suspicious. When Slobodan Milosevic died, it was suspicious to me. Even then, I addressed the President of the Tribunal by separate motion. The motion can be found in the archives, so that I wouldn't be speaking about this if you hadn't mentioned the letter by Boris Aleksic, and it was sent to you for your information only, and not as a motion which you will decide upon. It's meant to be a piece of information for you and your colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Seselj, I take note of what you said. And in order to give you full information, as well as to help Mr. Marcussen, I will send a memo to the President of the Tribunal regarding the content of the letter written by Mr. Boris Aleksic, reminding him of the number of deaths that have occurred here, and I will tell him the following, and I will say, I quote: It will be useful to appoint an independent commission in order to do this groundwork and to shed light on this matter. This is my position, and this is what I'll say to the President of the Tribunal. It will then be up to him to do what he deems fit. I have hesitated between two solutions or two options. Either I could have forwarded the letter directly to the Secretary-General of the United Nations or I could have contacted the President of the Tribunal. I felt it was more fit to contact the President of the Tribunal, and this is exactly what I'm going to do. Could you perhaps move on to another topic, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one more sentence. This letter mattered to me just because of the letter drafted by Ken Roberts, who threatened my legal adviser and threatened him to cut his privileged communication lines with me. That's what matters for me. You mentioned here that the Trial Chamber is waiting for an expert report about the authenticity of the diaries of General Ratko Mladic. From the point of view of the interests of my defence, it doesn't matter at all whether these diaries are authentic or not. I said that I doubted the authenticity of these diaries and that I had reasons for doubting it. The police searched the house of General Mladic several times, and how come they have just now found the diaries, without having found them earlier? But let's leave that aside. Even if it should turn out that the diaries are authentic, what has that got to do with this trial? You saw what the Prosecution found in these diaries which, according to them, can be used in this trial. Absolutely nothing. Nothing there incriminates me or makes my position more difficult, anything. It's totally irrelevant. But the problem is that we are losing so many months over that. Instead of July, under Rule 98 bis -- Mr. Marcussen and I have been waiting for being heard under Rule 98 bis still, and who knows how long we're going to wait still, and who knows whether we will ever complete our work under 98 bis: That's what the essence is. The essence is that we are unnecessarily wasting time in this trial over Mladic's alleged diaries, and we wasted time earlier. Months are passing, years are passing, and the more time elapses with me in detention and the longer this trial lasts, the less regular this trial is. If I had defended myself as a free man for eight years, even so my right to be tried within a reasonable time-frame would have been violated. Even if I had been a free man all this while, if I had come from Belgrade for each hearing, even then my right to be tried in a reasonable time-frame would have been blatantly violated, but especially -- it's especially so now, because I've been in detention for eight years. In America, even those accused of multiple murder have to be released if a reasonable time-period has elapsed. There is no lawyer alive who can responsibly claim that this trial is going on for a reasonable time, especially given the fact that the Defence case is still ahead of us, and then there will be appeals, and the trial will overall probably last for over 20 years. You mentioned Witness 026. This complicates things further. According to my information, the witness recovered pretty well after the last phase of his treatment. He is not as robust as I am, but he's fully capable of testifying, especially if he will testify by videolink. He is a Prosecution witness. He's important to the Prosecution, to the Trial Chamber, and he's important to me, if nothing else so that he can explain to me here, in this courtroom, how come I blew up the Roman Catholic cathedral in Subotica, which is still standing and has never been blown up by anybody. It's just that I want to make clear, and then we don't need to speak about anything else. And how come that such statements went through the hands of the Prosecutors, and who created all that? There is also some dark force here. The Prosecutor may call this a theory of conspiracy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a second, Mr. Seselj. In case of VS-026 testifying, he would testify on what is in the case. You could not ask questions as to which conditions were prevailing when his statement was taken, because this is the sole competency of the amicus curiae, and, therefore, the Judges are not in a position to touch upon this issue. It is solely for the amicus curiae to deal with that. So if he testifies, he will testify on the merits of the case, the cathedral, the volunteers, the war, and so on and so forth, but not on the conditions, because this is not in our realm of competency. My colleague points out --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judges, you cannot prevent me from challenging a witness's credibility. I can examine that in a positive and negative sense. I can affirm his testimony, I can examine him that way, and I can examine him in another way, by denying his testimony. I have been studying Anglo-Saxon legal procedure here for eight years. It never would have crossed my mind, while I was still a free man, and now I've become an expert in this field. As for this Roman Catholic cathedral, that will have to be discussed. It's part of his previous statement. It has to be discussed, whether it was blown up or not and what actually happened there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I suggest we wait until the witness is here to discuss the issue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I understand you, and I fully agree with that, Mr. Harhoff. But I have this other problem now in relation to this witness. I have the impression, because now I have information - I am no longer forbidden from contacting this witness. ^ I am informed about where they are taking him now, to various examinations by specialists to see whether he is capable of testifying or not. At the Military Medical Academy, they refused to examine him because they didn't know who would pay for that. Then they took him to the St. Sava Hospital in Belgrade, and that is a hospital for treating brain and blood vessel ailments. Of course, it does have something to do with it vaguely; cardiovascular conditions, but it does specialise in brain and blood vessel ailments, and you could always find a doctor there who would sign a statement saying that he could not testify. There is some dark force in Belgrade that is trying to prevent this witness from testifying, so I'm saying to you that if it so happens that if you get some kind of an opinion from Belgrade, a medical opinion, stating that he cannot testify, that has to be reviewed, because that witness can truly testify. He really is in a position to do so. We've already agreed that it can be done by videolink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, let's move to closed session. I believe that this is why Mr. Marcussen is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour, and I believe we would also need a small redaction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Closed session, please. Closed session, please, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, are you finished or do you still have points on the agenda?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is the first topic that you started off with at this administrative hearing today, and that is the question of financing the Defence. First of all, in the text of your decision, there is a problem. There is a reference to this being a confidential document, with confidential and ex parte annexes of the two parties. I did not receive any ex parte annexes. Since it is only the disposition that is given in public, I assume that it is, therefore, public. You read the disposition, and I'm only going to deal with that. I don't know why the entire text of the decision has been declared a confidential document when everything there had to be public, but perhaps you have some reason for that. Also, I have not received the separate opinion of Judge Lattanzi, and I'm very sorry about that, because I'm sure that Judge Flavia Lattanzi was far more inclined towards the interest of my Defence than the majority of the Trial Chamber. But I hope that I will receive this separate opinion and that I'm going to use it to buttress my argument in further proceedings. There is a dilemma here. When speaking of the amount, as stated here, that is usually allocated to indigent accused persons, what is unclear is whether it is an amount -- it is an amount that is given in every particular case there is no Defence team -- or where there is a Defence team and where there is a lawyer, and then 50 per cent of that, or is it 50 per cent of the sum that is received, say, by Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Tolimir? That would be senseless. However, I have to tell you, although I do not intend to appeal this decision at all, it is inapplicable, as far as my Defence team is concerned, because it says here that financial assistance, two legal advisers, to the investigator and case manager, will be paid as of today in the future. Without any retroactive payments for the Defence over these past eight years, my legal advisers will not agree to any kind of payments in the future either. And then you know full well what kind of effect this will have in terms of presenting the Defence case. In that situation, we will not be able to present a Defence case. I am only going to confine myself to an opening statement of the Defence. That is what I'm entitled to. The Prosecutor had an opening statement of four hours, and I hope that you are going to give me equal time, because when I used four hours when the Prosecutor spoke, that was a statement by the accused. Those were -- that was not an opening statement, and that's how we treated it. But now I'm going to be entitled to opening argument by the Defence, and if there is no retroactive payment given to cover the costs of the Defence, we are going to complete these proceedings very quickly. Of course, Rule 98 bis can allow us to go on and procrastinate for another year, but I would like these proceedings to be brought to an end while I'm still alive. I know that there are many of those who would not want these proceedings to end while I'm still alive, because that solution would be far simpler. However, I want to be fully victorious in these proceedings, and it's obvious to one and all that I'm only a step away from that victory. Judges, even if you want to declare me guilty and condemn me, you are fully aware of the fact that you have nothing upon which you could base such a decision and such a verdict, so that's -- and that is what the international public is aware of too. That's what I wanted to say to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I advise you to read this decision as soon as it is translated. I hope it will be perfectly translated, because in all the paragraphs before the disposition, we explain how we came to this decision. In the public version, there are a few redacted excerpts which have to do with elements that are not to be made public outside this Trial Chamber, but the reasoning is public. And you know that French is a very specific language, a very accurate language, just like yours, actually. Every word has its meaning. So read it fully. And let me tell you that it took us a very long time to write this decision. You know, we weighted every word, every comma, and it took us quite some time to render the decision, but it is very comprehensive, everything is included. But you have to read it after a good night's rest because it is difficult to comment on this off the cuff without having the text.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, recently I received these confidential documents. I won't go into their contents. I received a letter from you, sent to the Prosecutor, or addressed to him. I received it in French. I don't speak French, and I received a translation of that letter. In other words, I'm not a chicken, I cannot lay eggs, but I can tell if it's a bad egg or a good one. This shows that a large portion of your letter was left out in the translation, it's missing. Even the previous sentence is not translated as it should be. So it's obvious, at first sight, that it's a bad translation. You may ask the usher to give this to you so you can ascertain after this hearing that what I'm saying is true. So possibly you can send this to me once more, because this is important for my documentation. So you can see what kind of problems I'm facing with translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I will check whether my letter was well translated, and if there are parts of it that are missing, it will be -- it will be completed. But I don't know your language, so as of now I cannot say whether this was fully translated or not. But let me tell you that we will do all the necessary checks. Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I think, in light of some of the things that have been said today, I can be briefer than I had expected, which is a good thing. I thought, first of all, I should just put on record that I agree with the accused's submissions about the scope of examination of VS-26 when it comes to the issue of use of statements and testing the credibility of witnesses. The accused has very much expressed a view which is similar to ours; namely, that these issues of credibility of witnesses who appear before the Court are key issues that have to be dealt with in this Chamber and cannot be out-sourced to an amicus curiae. So there might be -- there might be -- there is going to be an investigation of members of the Office of the Prosecutor, and that has to run its course, obviously. As has been stated several times by the Prosecutor, the Office of the Prosecutor will co-operate fully with that investigation. But the issues that are raised with respect to the credibility of admitted evidence in the case still have to be tested -- have to be dealt with in the context of the case, and the credibility issues have to be settled here. So the Prosecution's position is very much similar to that of the accused; namely, that the evidentiary issues that have been raised by the allegations that have been made in court by witnesses must be tested by the Court. That will apply to VS-26, and that is why the Prosecution have made a request -- requests for leave to amend its witness list and call witnesses who can give evidence about a number of these issues. So I just wanted to put that on record. I appreciate the remark that has been made, that this is something we will come back to in the context of VS-26, if VS-26 is actually going to come.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Marcussen, very well. I take due note of what you said, and I'm very glad to hear that you have the same -- you are of the same opinion as Mr. Seselj on this issue. And the Trial Chamber will deliberate on this, but I would like you to shed some light on an issue for me. I would like you, Mr. Marcussen, to tell us when it's a Chamber witness, because this is a Chamber witness, a Court witness. I believe that in our -- in the practice of this Tribunal - I will not mention any cases - but I believe that the Trial Chamber, since it's its own witness, can limit -- very strictly limit the scope of the examination. And unless I'm wrong, furthermore -- but, I mean, I've been here for seven years, so I don't think I'm wrong -- the way a witness is to be examined is controlled by the Judges at all times. So what do you have to say to this? If you could shed some light on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think there are two -- there are two issues. As to the Judges' powers to regulate the examination of witnesses and the modalities of how witnesses testify before the Chamber, it is obvious that the Trial Chamber retain powers to do so. But the question that the Prosecution is raising is the fair trial rights of the parties to be able to test fully the evidence before the Tribunal, and that means that the parties must be allowed to present evidence and arguments as to the reliability and credibility of all evidence that's being presented before the Court. We have understood, from things -- a number of remarks that have been made in court and from decisions that have been rendered, that the Trial Chamber will be using the investigation as a means to test the reliability of the -- of statements that have been admitted into evidence or that have been tendered by the Prosecution. That is what we say cannot be done. The Prosecution's position is that the evidence has to be presented in court. The parties have the right to make submissions on the impact of that evidence, and the testing of the credibility and the taking of evidence which might be relevant to the assessment of credibility of evidence in the case cannot be out-sourced to someone else. It is the core purpose of the trial to test the evidence in the case. It simply cannot be done outside the trial process. That's the Prosecution's position, and that is why we have requested leave to amend our witness list so that we can call witnesses who can give evidence about a number of the issues that have been raised. And what is going to happen when VS-26 is going to testify, we don't know. Maybe it is not going to become an issue. But if it is, what I'm saying is we fully agree with the accused that he will be entitled and we will be entitled to explore all issues that arise in that context. If allegations, again, are going to be made about how these statements were obtained, whether they are correct or whether they are not correct. And it is a normal step in any trial that if issues arise as to whether or not allegations of that nature are true, investigators or other people with knowledge of these facts can be called, and we submit they should be called in this case. And the fact that there's an investigation, well, that's a separate matter. It cannot replace the testing of the evidence in this case. That is the core of some of the issues that we have raised --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... I'm not saying that the Judges do not have the power to control the examination of witnesses. That's obvious.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Marcussen, the Judges will deliberate on this, of course, and you have expressed your opinion. As of now, I cannot answer. We first have to deliberate on this. And when Witness VS-26 will testify, then the Trial Chamber will say exactly what it expects. But we took due note of what you just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I was going to make a request that the Trial Chamber's decision regarding the funding of the Defence be made public. I understand there's a redacted version. We haven't seen that yet, so maybe there is no issue. I just wanted to point, today, the Court's attention to the decision of 20th January 2004 in the Krajisnik case, which is a public decision, which sets out its reasoning for why Mr. Krajisnik should pay part of his Defence himself. And I'm not bringing this up because of the substance of the decision but simply to point out that, in the practice of the Tribunal, these sort of decisions have been public. We submit that the public should be allowed to understand the reasons of the Chamber, and certainly in light of all the times these issues have come up in the case and have been raised both by the accused and the Judges. But we will see what the redacted version looks like, and maybe there is no issue. I was going to address also scheduling issues. I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Marcussen, you will also have the confidential version, of course. It's not ex parte, so you will be entitled to have the full reasoning behind the decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... I'm talking about the public's access to the Trial Chamber's reasoning. We have received the confidential version. Obviously, we haven't received the ex parte parts of it, but we are informed of the full reasoning of the Chamber. I'm sorry if there was any confusion on that point. As for scheduling issues, it sounds like a lot of decisions will be coming shortly. We tried to count, on the Prosecution side, on the number of pending motions before today, and our understanding -- we came to the number of 14 motions, which I guess then mean there might be 6 motions still to be ruled on, but maybe this is something that can be co-ordinated with the Legal Officer if there's an issue there. I'm not going to address scheduling any more, other than just asking clarification on one point. Do I understand correctly that one of the scheduling -- one of the motions that will be ruled on shortly is the Prosecution request for leave to add additional witnesses to its witness list? I see the Judge's nod, so that is the case. Then I will leave the remaining scheduling issues out. There's two more issues left that we would like to address. One is some of the issues that arise out of the Trial Chamber's decision regarding the Mladic note-books and some issues that arise out of the medical examination decision. I will be addressing the first issue, and Ms. Biersay will be addressing the second. Regarding the Mladic note-books, I'm going to say a little bit about the material that has been tendered by the Prosecution, make some remarks about the expert and handling of evidence, and address disclosure. In reading the Trial Chamber's decision from the 22nd of October, it appears that there might be cause --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have an objection. I demand that Mr. Marcussen delay these requests or proposals or suggestions until the next hearing on the administrative issues, because I haven't received the relevant documents yet and I cannot follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Marcussen, it seems that Mr. Seselj has not received all the Trial Chamber's decisions so far, but maybe you can sum up the substance of the decision. That way, Mr. Seselj will be fully informed. Or I could do it myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Surely, Your Honours. And I want to be clear so the accused appreciates what I'm doing. I'm not making submissions as to the admissibility of the note-books or addressing the merit of the decision, and I'm not -- I'm actually not going to make any requests. I'm more addressing a number of issues, which might be informative also to the accused once he gets the decision. Basically, the Trial Chamber has ordered two things relevant --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judges, I've been listening to Mr. Marcussen carefully, and I insist that he put forward his opinion and his information once I get the decision so that I can follow. There's no point in him going on about this here without me having the faintest idea what it's about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Seselj, as you know, following to what you said to us regarding the Mladic diaries, the Trial Chamber appointed an expert. If I had known that this topic was going to be touched upon, I would have brought with me the decision, but I'm sure that the Legal Officer has the decision here. In our decision, we said that we were asking an expert -- there we go. Thank you, Mr. Marcussen, for giving me what the Legal Officer should have given me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... see if it's actually the right compilation of materials, because there might be more in the bundle so maybe I can put it up to you at the right page. Actually, my case manager is printing a copy for you now, and I think it's coming to -- to me, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, Mr. Seselj, I'm going to read the disposition, bearing in mind that I also have a separate opinion of 28 pages. And I'm not going to read the 28 pages on the issue. I'm only going to read out to you the disposition, which sums up the unanimous position of this Trial Chamber, and I should like to point this out. My separate opinion is a separate opinion which actually goes in the same line as the general opinion, but it's a 28-page opinion, and again I suggest that you read it carefully once it's translated into your language, of course. Since the OTP is very efficient, they are going to provide me with my decision. I'm really sorry, I should have brought it with me. I'm really sorry. Usually, I bring everything with me. But I have to say that I didn't do this because I didn't realise that we would come back to the Mladic diaries and that we would revisit this issue, and I made a mistake. And I would like to apologise to the parties, because we are wasting time here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: The Prosecution wasn't able to be as efficient as we had hoped. But, fortunately, the Registrar is very efficient, so I believe he now has the decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. So this is what I'm saying in a disposition: "Orders the Prosecution to disclose to the accused a typewritten hard copy in B/C/S of the entire Mladic note-books." So, Mr. Seselj, you should receive a hard copy of the note-books: "Grants the Prosecution's request to add the documents mentioned in the motion to the 65 ter exhibit list. "Grants the Prosecution's request to add Milanovic and Gallagher to the 65 ter witness list. "Grants the Prosecution's request for admission into evidence of the Milanovic statement and the Gallagher, in accordance with Rule 92 bis of the Rules. "Defers the ruling on the request for the admission of extracts from the Mladic note-books. "Orders the Registry to appoint an independent expert, whose task will be to read, in the original version, the extracts of the Mladic note-books whose admission is sought. "To determine whether General Mladic is the author by comparing them to other documents written by General Mladic in the same period whose source and date are certain, known, and reliable. "To highlight any amendment, addition, or deletion that might have occurred to the documents under examination. "If possible, to determine whether some of the entries were written at intervals over several years by comparing them with other documents whose source and date are certain, written by General Mladic at different times, starting with 1991, and; "To inform the Chamber of any other relevant information with regard to the documents under examination. "The appointed expert shall provide the Chamber with an expert report by no later than 15th of December, 2010. "Orders the Prosecution to hand over immediately the original copies of the Mladic note-books, together with any other document that might be necessary for the successful completion of the task upon request from the appointed expert. "Presiding Judge Antonetti attaches a separate opinion to this decision." As I said, this separate opinion is 28 pages long, and I'm not going to read it out, even if it was very interesting. Yes, Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Would the Chamber like us to have a break before I start or is it not quite time yet?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if you are very quick, perhaps we can conclude without any break. And, of course, Mr. Seselj has to have a rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution tendered a rather limited amount of material when it tendered its evidence relating to the Mladic note-books. And reading the Trial Chamber's decision, that it seems that might have given rise to some confusion and also maybe to an impression that the Prosecution is withholding relevant evidence from the Trial Chamber, which certainly is not the case. The Prosecution, in light of the late stage of the proceeding, has made an effort to limit the amount of evidence that we tendered in relation to the Mladic note-books, so we limited ourselves to a few extracts and to the evidence of two witnesses. This was not done in any way to try to keep anything from the Trial Chamber, but simply to try to be efficient. Now, one of the -- there are two points I would like to just clarify so there is not confusion about the material that has been tendered. One thing is: In paragraph 33 of the decision, it is stated that the Witness Mihajlovic [sic] did not recognise the handwriting in certain parts of note-book number 18. That is not the case. Milovanovic looked at a scanned range of material -- sorry, it should be "Milovanovic," in line 4 of page 42. That is not the case, Your Honours. The witness Milovanovic looked at a scanned bundle of documents. That document included a note-book and then other material. And among that other material were a number of documents which are not part of a note-book and which clearly have been written by someone else, and it is not the Prosecution's position that these other materials are part of a note-book, nor that they bear Mladic's handwriting. For example, there are letters. One is a letter that is written in the Latin script and not in Cyrillic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Marcussen, I really don't want to interfere with this, but I think it would be prudent, perhaps, to reserve these questions until there is the declaration from the expert, because only then we would be able to determine what to make of Milovanovic's decision. At this point, it's really open, and unless you have any strong needs to invoke this at this moment, I suggest we drop it. But I'm not sure of the reasons why you are raising it, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: The reason I'm raising, and that's what I'm getting to now, is that when the expert gets material, he will not get to see -- he or she will not get to see these other things. This other material is not part of the note-books. So the point I'm clarifying is that the actual note-books do not contain these other documents which do not bear -- which have someone else's handwriting on them. So when we provide note-books to the accused -- to the expert, that material isn't going to be there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But, Mr. Marcussen, the decision only suggests that the note-books be submitted to the expert, and nothing else. [Interpretation] "The Chamber orders the Registry to appoint an independent expert, whose task will be to read, in the original version, the excerpt of the Mladic note-books whose admission is sought." In other words, no other submission will be made, no other documents handwritten by Mr. Mladic. We're only talking about the Mladic diaries, so I hope that there is no confusion regarding that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: The disposition, we understand, and we will submit only the note-books. There seemed to be a confusion in paragraph 33 of the decision, though, because there it is stated that there were parts of Note-book 18 which Milovanovic was not able to identify as being written by Mr. Mladic, and that it was someone else's handwriting. The point I'm making is --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- I have to intervene. What is being debated here are things that I am not versed with at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, I think it has been said already by yourself --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can it be all right if the Prosecutor interrupts me all the time and I cannot interrupt him? He interrupts me all the time, and whenever Mr. Marcussen is on his feet, you give him the floor. And now he's complaining because I am interrupting him. I am not providing counter-arguments. I'm not interrupting him that way. I'm just raising an objection. I'm saying that he is speaking about things that I don't know of at all, and could all of this be halted until I've been given a copy of your decision?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Marcussen, you mentioned paragraph 33 of a document which the accused does not have, so there is an issue here. Judge Harhoff said that it was premature and that we should wait until the expert opinion has come back to us in order to state your position. And I believe that Judge Lattanzi also wants to take the floor. But before I give her the floor, you are mentioning that in paragraph 33 we are talking about pages that would not have been handwritten by Mr. Mladic, but you can also send to the expert what you want to send to him as part of the decision from this Chamber. So you are raising an issue which I believe is non-existent. And if the expert has any problem with that, perhaps this person would be able to contact you, because you have stated in the disposition that the expert could be in the position to also make comments on other things. So they can also provide the Chamber with any other information that would be useful to be examined. So what you're raising, if the expert feels that there is an issue, they will say something. I give the floor to Judge Lattanzi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Marcussen, I would like to have some clarification on one point. I would like to know: What is the purpose of your submission here? Do you want the Trial Chamber to give some clarification on the decision or do you want the Trial Chamber to reconsider its decision? I don't quite understand the purpose of why you have taken the floor right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: The Prosecution does not want there to be any misapprehension as to what material we understand is covered by the decision, and we would wish to clarify what appeared to be perhaps a misunderstanding, which might have been caused by the Prosecution, but a misunderstanding as to what material Mr. -- General Milovanovic has looked at, what is part of the note-books and what is not. If the Chamber thinks that there is a note-book which we will be providing to the expert, and that note-book contains seven pages which have been written, according to the witness, by someone else, then that is not the case. I hope that's clear. What I -- there are a number of other issues. Maybe the best is, and also in light of what the accused has said, is we will be addressing these issues in writing so there is no misapprehension of what the process is going to be. I would like to point out at this stage that we would also be addressing some practical issues about how this evidence has to be handled. The Mladic note-books are -- it's admitted evidence in other cases. It's potentially evidence in the case against Mladic, should he get arrested. A number of technical precautions have been taken to preserve the evidence, and the Prosecution will corroborate with the appointed handwriting expert, but there will be technical issues that have been to addressed. It is not just a question of the Office of the Prosecutor taking these originals out of its evidence collection and hand it to an expert, who can go out somewhere, do his or her analysis of the evidence, and come back with an opinion. There would also be issues about potentially finding a sample that can be used for comparison. We will address these things in a written filing, but I want to reassure the Chamber that we do this not in the spirit of hampering what the Chamber has ordered, but there are some real, practical evidentiary precautions that have to be taken, and I'm sure the Trial Chamber fully appreciate that as well as the Prosecution does, and there are issues -- well, let me not get into that now, but there are a number of real, practical issues that we would have to deal with very carefully in light of the nature of this evidence. And what we would be suggesting is once the expert is assigned, that the Prosecution be provided the CV of the expert and is given an outline of what the expert would like to do with this material so we can work with the expert to find a way in which the examination of this sensitive material can be done in a way which does not prejudice its evidentiary status in other cases. So I just seize this occasion to bring it up. We will, as I say, address you in writing on this, but there are some issues that we will have to address. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Marcussen, I fully understood what you just said, and I fully understand that you are not planning to hand over the original documents and then there is a burglary at the expert's premises and everything disappears. I fully understood you. You do not have to even go as far as primary school to understand that. And I'm sure that with the expert that will have been appointed, you will make sure that the evidence is preserved with the help of the Office of the Prosecutor. But you're fully aware that an expert can only work on original documents. Therefore, at some stage he will have to -- he or she will need to have a look at the original documents. Perhaps this can be looked at within the premises of the Tribunal, but this is something that you can look into with him or her. We are talking about highly technical issues here, and, in fact, I suggest that you read the 58 pages that I have written in another case, and the 28 pages that I have written for this case, in order to understand what is an expert opinion. But I'm sure that your fears will be alleviated. Mr. Marcussen, we are beyond the time that was allocated to us for the first session, so don't you think that we should have a break in order to resume later on? I believe that Mr. Seselj wants to take the floor. So we're going to have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: Mr. Marcussen, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, we will make efforts to assist you in determining what material is actually on the internet and get back to you. We should not, maybe, take up time here now with that. Your Honours, I just have one brief more piece of information, maybe, and then I'll hand over to Ms. Biersay. The Prosecution was ordered to disclose to the accused the transcripts of the Mladic note-books. I don't know whether the accused has received that material yet, but we -- it has been sent off from us. So he would get it today, if he hasn't received it. But I want to clarify that the Prosecution has transcribed only the note-books that were seized this year. So the five note-books that were seized last year, there is no transcription of those. We have not prepared that, and, therefore, that material has not been disclosed. Sorry, I'm getting it wrong. It was two years ago, not last year. But my point basically is that we have disclosed what we have transcribed, that has been given to the accused, but it does not cover the five first note-books because we have not prepared transcriptions for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Marcussen, have you submitted the parts that you seek tendered into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Already when we tendered the excerpts that we wanted to propose as evidence in the case, that was provided back then in hard copy to the accused already, so we're talking -- right. And none of the excerpts we have tendered come from the first seizure. The excerpts that we have selected are only from the new seizure of material. I just wanted to clarify that so it's clear what has been disclosed to the accused. Of course, all the material is available on the EDS, the Electronic Disclosure Suite, on all that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: That is to say, for the photocopies of the entire --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone for the Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Sorry. Can we just clarify that photocopies of the entire set of note-books is available on the EDS? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour, scanned -- scanned versions of it, yes. I'll hand over to Ms. Biersay if there's nothing else on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Biersay, good afternoon. We haven't heard you for a while, and it's a great pleasure for me to give you the floor once again.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: May I please request that we go into private session to discuss a short matter pertaining to VS-026.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, could we move to private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. As Mr. Marcussen indicated, I am going to very, very briefly address the issue of the medical assessments that have been ordered proprio motu by the Trial Chamber, and specifically the Prosecution respectfully requests that, as has been done in other cases, that it be given the material underlying the Trial Chamber's orders about those medical assessments, and that is so that the Prosecution can fully exercise its rights to be informed and to be heard regarding these issues. Now, I am quite sure that the Trial Chamber is aware of another case before the Tribunal, in the Stanisic/Simatovic case, and in that case the health of one of the accused was a central issue, specifically as it pertained to the accused's ability to stand trial and also the scheduling and modalities of that trial. In that case, it was the accused who made a motion that resulted in the litigation of health-related issues, and in that case the relevant medical reports and assessments given to the Trial Chamber were also disclosed to the Prosecution. In that case, no decision on modality or fitness to stand trial, or even provisional release, none of those decisions were taken without the Trial Chamber first hearing from the Prosecution and the Defence. When reports in that case were submitted by the reporting medical officer on issues of modalities of the trial and fitness for trial, the Prosecution and the Defence were always afforded the opportunity to propose questions to put to the medical officer. Also, in that case, the Defence, the Prosecution and the Trial Chamber each had their experts contributing to the process of assessing that accused's health condition. This is a little bit different from where we stand today in this case, where I do not believe that Mr. Seselj has made a motion to the Trial Chamber for any kind of medical assessment and the decision was taken proprio motu by the Trial Chamber. Specifically, the Trial Chamber's orders, and I'm referring to primarily the one issued on October 19th, 2010, but there was also another that I won't go into -- that that order was based on information that the Prosecution has never received. And, finally, the Prosecution was given notice of the issue discussed in that order only after the order was issued. So for these reasons, we are asking that we be given the material that, I believe, until now has been dealt with in an ex parte fashion; namely, the reports on Mr. Seselj's health that have been given to the Trial Chamber. And I believe the Presiding Judge indicated that the purpose of the assessment was to make sure that Mr. Seselj, of course, remained healthy and that he remains able -- fit -- and that he remains fit for trial, and that he is able to represent himself, and these are all pertinent issues to both parties in the case. So for these reasons, we believe that it would be appropriate to disclose the underlying material on which the Trial Chamber relied to render its previous decisions so that we can meaningfully and fully exercise our right to be heard. Fairness would also require that both the Prosecution and the accused be given the opportunity to participate in a transparent process of selecting the members of the medical expert panel. Now, we're quite open to the modalities of how the parties can participate in the selection of the panel, but we are requesting that there be some participation by the parties in this process. And with that, I will end my comments. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Biersay -- just a minute, Mr. Seselj. I'll give you the floor in a minute. Ms. Biersay, when you're taking the floor, I'm always listening to you with great attention because what you're saying is always extremely interesting. I fully understood that the Prosecution wanted to be made aware of all the documents, all the underlying documents, and I'm 100 per cent in agreement with you. However, there is a small item that could lead to many discussions, but we're not going to open this today, this discussion today. You say that the Prosecution and the accused would like to participate in the appointment of the expert panel. It's quite attractive as an idea, you know. However, according to the Rules and the directives, as of today the Trial Chamber is entitled to decide that an expertise is required, that an expert evaluation is required, and the expert or the experts are to be appointed by the Registrar, who can consult the Chamber if it wishes to. Now, the Rules could have provided for what you want. You know, when there is to be an expert opinion, the parties can suggest their own experts to the Trial Chamber. It could have -- it could happen. Why not? But it's not stated in the Rules. Furthermore, you know that we are in a mixed system, with a combination of common law and civil law.
